cards.title: Build a Linked Acquisition-to-Retention Model for Transactional + Subscription Mix
cards.summary: Forecast ad-hoc and subscription customer streams separately so you can see how each drives revenue, profit and LTV in a blended subscription business.
cards.use_when: Financial planning for a store selling both one-time purchases and subscriptions (subscription box, supplements, consumables) where you need to model growth, breakeven and cash needs.
steps: Split new customers into transactional vs subscription each month, and transition the split over time: source's scenario starts at 60% transactional / 40% subscription in months 1-3, moves to 50/50 in months 4-6, and settles at 30/70 after a default-to-subscription cart change.

Model transactional repeat purchasing with a rolling return rate: divide returning customers last month by total customers acquired in the trailing 6 months. Source's example uses ~3.3% of the 6-month customer base returning in any given month.
Apply that return rate to the trailing 6-month customer count month by month, growing the trailing window as the store accumulates history.

Model subscriptions with a monthly churn rate, applied to the prior month's active subscriber base (not to this month's new signups). Source uses 25% monthly churn as a conservative subscription-box assumption.

Compute subscription lifetime orders as 1 / churn rate (25% churn = 4 orders), and transactional lifetime orders via the geometric series 1 / (1 - annual retention rate). Source's 40% annual retention gives ~1.7 lifetime orders.

Feed each stream's orders through separate AOV, refund/discount and per-unit COGS assumptions to produce revenue, COGS, contribution margin and LTV, then consolidate into an income statement and compute the blended, conversion-weighted LTV.
Expose CAC, LTV, LTV/CAC and LTV-CAC per segment and blended; plan to revise CAC each month as real market data replaces assumptions.
caveats: The 3.3% return rate, 25% churn and stated split percentages are source-scenario illustrations, not benchmarks — backtest them against your own trailing data before relying on them.
Weighting blended LTV by conversion split rather than revenue share changes the result; state which basis you use.

cards.title: Forecast Marketing Spend into New Customers via CAC Assumptions
cards.summary: Convert a monthly ad budget into expected new customers by dividing spend by an assumed and iteratively updated CAC.
cards.use_when: Setting or pressure-testing monthly ad spend and growth targets for a store, and checking whether the acquired customers can ever be profitable.
steps: Set a CAC assumption per period — the source starts at $100 for the first few months, steps to $75 through month 12 and $60 thereafter in one scenario — and note that brands with strong organic can run far lower while niche paid-only brands run higher.
Divide monthly spend by CAC, rounded to a whole number, to get expected new customers (source example: $5,000 / $100 = 50 new customers).
Multiply forward across months to build the new-customer forecast, then push those customers into retention and subscription models to produce revenue.

As you scale, replace the assumption with observed CAC from your own market data and re-forecast, since CAC depends on copy, product, brand awareness and audience targeting and cannot be known before you go to market.
Check the resultant LTV against CAC — the source argues that if LTV is below CAC you lose money on every customer relationship and there is no viable business at that point.
caveats: The $100/$75/$60 ladder is a source-specific modeling example, not a benchmark; your CAC is only knowable after real market testing.
Blended CAC can mask segment differences — a profitable subscription cohort may subsidize an unprofitable transactional cohort.

cards.title: Use Trigger Events to Shift New Customers from One-Time to Subscription
cards.summary: Sequence offer, discount and cart-default changes over months to lift the subscription share of new customers toward a 30/70 steady state.
cards.use_when: Designing subscription upsell offers, discount structures and cart/checkout defaults for a store trying to move from mostly one-time sales to recurring revenue.
steps: Start with a strong subscribe-and-save offer at checkout to capture the easy subscribers — source scenario reaches ~40% subscription signups in months 1-3.
Strengthen the subscription offer further (months 4-6, target ~50%) and then shift discount strategy: remove or reduce discounts on one-time purchases and tilt discounts toward subscribers.

From roughly month 10 onward, default the cart to subscription so buyers must actively switch back to one-time purchase. The source reports about a 60-70% increase in new subscription signups when defaulting the cart to subscription (data from the source's own platform, OrderGroove).
Lock the resulting 30% transactional / 70% subscription new-customer split as the steady state and carry it through the rest of the model.
Verify the default-to-subscription and checkout options available in your current platform before planning this change, since interfaces differ and change.
caveats: The 60-70% uplift figure is the source's own platform data from defaulting carts to subscription — treat as an example, not a guaranteed result.
Aggressive defaults and asymmetric discounts can annoy customers or invite cancellations; the source does not quantify downside.

cards.title: Forecast Transactional Repeat Customers with a 6-Month Rolling Return Rate
cards.summary: Estimate how many one-time buyers return each month by applying a measured return rate to the trailing six months of acquired customers.
cards.use_when: Modeling repeat revenue and LTV for non-subscription customers where you cannot simply use 1/churn.
steps: Measure the historical return rate: total returning customers in a month divided by the total customers acquired over the trailing six months. The source typically sees figures like 3-5%.

Forecast forward by multiplying each month's trailing 6-month customer count by that rate, starting with only the data you actually have in early months and expanding the window to a full six months as history accrues.
Watch how the returning cohort accumulates: in the source's example, repeat transactional customers reach 576/month (vs 2,850 new) by month 36.
Convert the model into lifetime orders using the geometric series 1 / (1 - annual retention rate); the source's 3.3% monthly rate implies ~40% annual retention and ~1.7 lifetime orders.
Multiply lifetime orders by contribution margin per order (not revenue) to get transactional LTV — the source treats lifetime contribution margin as the meaningful LTV definition.
caveats: The rate must be measured from your own 6 months of data; 3.3% is the source's illustration.
The method assumes returning behaviour is reasonably stable; launches, seasonality or product changes can distort it.

cards.title: Compute Subscription Lifetime Orders from Monthly Churn
cards.summary: Derive average subscriber lifetime orders and LTV by dividing 1 by the churn rate, and show why subscriber LTV usually beats transactional LTV.
cards.use_when: Comparing subscriber versus one-time-buyer value to decide how hard to push subscription conversion and how much you can afford to spend acquiring subscribers.
steps: Pick a monthly churn assumption — the source uses 25% for a subscription box, noting it is common but conservative and that lower is better.
Calculate average lifetime orders as 1 / churn rate (25% churn implies 4 orders).
Multiply lifetime orders by the subscriber's contribution margin per order (source example: 4 orders x ~$33.70 = ~$134 subscriber LTV).
Compare with transactional LTV built from the geometric series method (source example: 1.7 orders x ~$55.70 = ~$93).
Feed both LTVs into a conversion-weighted blend (source example: $93 x 60% + $134 x 40% ≈ $109) and track how the blend rises as the subscriber mix grows.
Re-test the churn assumption against your own cohorts; conservative churn protects the model while better-than-assumed performance becomes upside.
caveats: 1/churn assumes a constant churn rate over the customer's life, which rarely holds exactly.
Subscribers often carry a lower contribution margin per order (bigger discount) even though lifetime value is higher — model both margin and lifetime, not just one.

cards.title: Report Post-Marketing Contribution Margin as the Core Profitability Gauge
cards.summary: Track contribution margin minus marketing each month to know whether the store can fund payroll and overhead at all.
cards.use_when: Monthly P&L review or investor reporting for any ecommerce store, especially when early customers are heavily first-time buyers.
steps: Compute contribution margin (revenue minus COGS) for the month, then subtract total marketing spend to get post-marketing contribution margin.
Interpret a negative figure as structurally unprofitable: the source's position is that if gross profit minus marketing is not positive, no amount of operating efficiency produces company profit.

Watch the trend rather than one month: in the source's scenario post-marketing contribution margin is negative early because there are few returning customers, and turns positive once the repeat/subscription base builds, because returning customers carry no CAC.
Use the metric to set the pace of hiring and overhead — payroll and other opex must fit under the post-marketing contribution margin for operating profit to exist.
Cross-check against LTV minus CAC as the unit-economics view of the same idea.
caveats: The source's timeline for reaching positive post-marketing contribution margin is scenario-specific and depends on retention build-up.
This is the source's strongly held operating view; it is a useful discipline, not a universal accounting rule.

cards.title: Build a Simple Bucketed Payroll and Opex Forecast
cards.summary: Forecast people costs by functional bucket and headcount, then layer non-payroll opex to reach operating income.
cards.use_when: Building or updating a store's operating expense forecast and finding the month where operating income turns positive.
steps: Define a few functional buckets that match how you actually staff — e.g. marketing, creative, operations, exec/admin — and put an average salary per bucket, since early-stage stores often keep marketing/creative in-house while outsourcing engineering and other functions.
Forecast headcount per bucket by month and multiply salary/12 by headcount, locking the salary column so the formula copies across months correctly.
Add ~25% on top of salary for benefits, taxes and similar costs to get true employee cost.
Forecast non-payroll opex accounts (other marketing/influencer work, consultants/1099s, software, miscellaneous) as manual line items and copy them across months.

Compute operating income (also called EBIT) as contribution margin minus all operating expenses; in the source's scenario operating income turns positive in month 17 and reaches a 19% EBIT margin by month 36.
Avoid bloated multi-tab, hundreds-of-rows payroll models unless genuinely necessary — the source recommends this quick bucketed approach instead.
caveats: The 25% loading and the month-17/19% margin outcomes are source-scenario assumptions, not benchmarks.
Outsourced vs in-house staffing mixes change the shape of this forecast; adjust buckets to your reality.

cards.title: Track the Cumulative Tax Loss Asset Before Assuming You Owe Tax
cards.summary: Accumulate operating losses so you can see how many months of profits are shielded before taxes apply.
cards.use_when: Cash planning and investor communications for an unprofitable-early store that is turning profitable, to avoid over-forecasting tax outflows.
steps: Track cumulative losses over time as a running total.

When modeling taxes, only apply the tax rate (source uses 25%) to profits once cumulative losses have been exhausted — the source's model shows no taxes due for roughly 11 months after first profitability.
Present the tax loss asset as an asset in the model since it offsets future taxable income.
Revisit if the business structure or jurisdiction changes, since tax loss carryforward rules vary.
Verify current tax treatment with a qualified accountant rather than relying on the model's simplification.
caveats: This is a simplified modeling convention; real tax loss carryforward rules and rates depend on jurisdiction and entity structure.
The 25% rate is a source example, not a universal or current rate.

cards.title: Forecast Inventory with Lead Time and Cycle Time Before You Model Cash
cards.summary: Work out when to place purchase orders by pairing supplier lead time with expected sell-through cycle, then cost each PO.
cards.use_when: Replenishment planning for any physical-product store to avoid stockouts and to see the true cash hit of inventory buys.
steps: Pull forecast order volumes from the demand model to know how many units each month must be fulfilled.
Set a lead time (source scenario: 3 months from order to receipt at the fulfillment center) and a cycle time (source scenario: 4 months of sell-through).
Order enough today so that inventory arriving after the lead time lasts through the cycle: order in month 1, receive in month 4, cover 4 months, then place the next PO.
Roll starting inventory minus orders each month, adding received POs when they land, to project inventory balances.
Cost each PO using a weighted-average product COGS across your order mix — the source weights transactional COGS ($7.70) and subscription COGS ($6.50) by order share to get ~$7.20 average.
Scale the PO cadence to reality (the source models quarterly-ish POs, but monthly POs may be needed) and stress-test demand because you are committing cash months before revenue.
caveats: Lead and cycle times are supply-chain specific; the source's 3-month lead and 4-month cycle are illustrative.
A single-SKU simplification is used — more SKUs multiply complexity substantially.

cards.title: Build a Mini Cash Flow Statement to Find Working Capital Needs and Runway
cards.summary: Reconcile net income with inventory purchases to project real cash burn and how much capital the store must raise.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much funding or cash buffer the store needs and when, especially for inventory-heavy CPG or subscription-box businesses.
steps: Start from net income, then subtract the cash actually paid out for inventory purchases in the month (the inventory bought but not yet sold).
Add back the product COGS of the units sold that month, because that cash went out earlier — the income statement matches cost to revenue, but cash timing differs.
Add any starting capital (source scenario begins with $500k raised) and roll the cash balance month by month.
Expect cash to be choppier than net income: the source's example shows cash going negative around month 8 and again needing a large inventory outlay shortly after.

Use the trough of the cash curve to size the raise: in the source's example, the business needed roughly $1-1.5M cumulative to reach profitability even though operating income turned positive earlier.
Separately note the store's revenue run rate (last month's revenue x 12) as a real-time pacing metric alongside trailing 12-month actuals, and be explicit which one you quote.
caveats: This mini cash flow ignores other assets and liabilities by design — it is not a full three-statement model.
Capital need figures are the source's scenario and depend heavily on lead times, payment terms and growth rate.

cards.title: Gross Revenue to Net Revenue Bridge: Report Refunds and Discounts Separately
cards.summary: Show gross revenue, then refunds/returns, then discounts, then net revenue — and split net revenue between first-time and repeat customers.
cards.use_when: Designing the monthly reporting pack or income statement presentation so you can see how much revenue discounts and refunds consume.
steps: Start with gross revenue from transactions times undiscounted AOV (source example: $2,700 AOV).
Subtract the refund/return rate (source assumes 4%) to quantify give-back.
Subtract discounts to arrive at net revenue, applying the appropriate net AOV per segment — the source notes subscription AOV is lower than one-time AOV.

Split net revenue into first-time vs returning/subscription-repeat revenue so you can see recurring revenue growing over time and shifting to the majority of the business (source scenario crosses to over 80% subscription revenue by month 36).
Use the split to verify your strategic direction: in a subscription business, repeat subscription revenue should eventually dwarf both first-time subscriptions and transactional revenue.
caveats: The 4% refund rate and AOV figures are the source's scenario assumptions.
Net revenue per segment requires segment-specific AOVs; using a blended AOV will misstate segment economics.

cards.title: Reconcile Your Model: Gross Profit Percentage Must Match Unit Economics
cards.summary: Use the gross profit rate as an arithmetic check that every revenue and COGS line is forecast correctly.
cards.use_when: After building or editing a financial model, before presenting numbers to investors or using them for decisions.
steps: Compute the blended gross profit percentage from the rolled-up income statement (revenue minus COGS, divided by revenue).
Compare it to the gross profit percentage implied by the bottom-up unit economics (AOV minus per-unit COGS and fees).
If they don't match by segment (the source checks transactional and subscription separately), you have a formula or referencing error somewhere in the model — find and fix it.
Repeat this check each time you change AOV, discount, refund or COGS assumptions.

Track blended gross margin alongside segment margins, since a mix shift toward subscriptions (lower gross margin percentage but higher lifetime value) can lower blended margin while improving the business.
caveats: A match confirms internal consistency, not that your assumptions are correct — wrong-but-consistent inputs still produce a wrong model.

cards.title: Consolidate Segments and Report the Ecommerce KPI Set
cards.summary: Roll transactional and subscription segments into one business view and report a fixed monthly KPI set to spot direction, not just level.
cards.use_when: Monthly management or investor reporting for a mixed one-time/subscription store; setting which numbers get tracked every month.
steps: Sum orders, gross revenue, net revenue, COGS and contribution margin across both segments to get the company total (source example reaches ~$1.6M net revenue per month by month 36).
Report annualized run rate (monthly revenue x 12) at the top, alongside trailing-12-month actuals, and be explicit which is which — the source prefers quoting run rate as the real-time pacing metric.
Report the subscription vs transactional revenue split and track it flipping toward subscription (source target: 80%+ subscription revenue).
Report CAC, blended LTV, LTV/CAC and LTV minus CAC per segment and weighted average.
Report post-marketing contribution margin and operating income/EBIT margin as the profitability lines.
Watch the LTV/CAC ratio trend: the source's scenario starts at 1.09 (barely above breakeven given the assumed CAC) and reaches 2 by month 36 through falling CAC and a richer subscription mix.
caveats: The source does not label 1.09 vs 2 as industry benchmarks; they are that scenario's trajectory.
Blended LTV requires a stated weighting basis (conversion mix vs revenue mix), or the ratio is ambiguous.
